claims.claim: Occupational health is an area of work in public health to promote and maintain the highest degree of physical, mental and social well-being of workers in all occupations (WHO working definition).

The WHO objectives of occupational health include maintaining and promoting workers' health and working capacity, improving working conditions and the working environment, and developing work organizations and working cultures conducive to safety and health.
The field of occupational health draws on several disciplines, including occupational medicine, nursing, ergonomics, psychology, hygiene, and safety.

Workplace health risks include physical hazards such as heat, noise, and radiation, which can cause hearing problems and other harm; MedlinePlus lists hearing problems caused by noise exposure among occupational health problems.
Chemical hazards include hazardous chemicals, dusts, and fumes; MedlinePlus describes illness caused by breathing, touching, or swallowing unsafe substances as an occupational health problem.
Biological hazards include germs; MedlinePlus names exposure to germs in health care settings as an occupational health problem.

Ergonomic hazards include repetitive motion and manual handling; the WHO fact sheet names ergonomic risks among occupational risks and MedlinePlus lists repetitive motion disorders among occupational health problems.

Psychosocial hazards include psychological stress, long hours, and the demands of work organization; the WHO fact sheet names psychological stress as a workplace health risk and protection from physical and psychosocial hazards as an effect of good working conditions.

The hierarchy of controls orders actions by general effectiveness: elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, and personal protective equipment; elimination removes the hazard at the source and is preferred because no exposure can occur.
Under federal law, the employer must keep the workplace free from known safety and health hazards, and workers have the right to workplace safety and health training in a language they understand.
OSHA's mission is to ensure workers have safe and healthful working conditions by setting and enforcing standards and providing training, outreach, education, and assistance.
Medical screening and medical surveillance are established workplace health-protection measures; OSHA maintains medical screening and surveillance requirements for certain hazards.

The WHO fact sheet calls for medical surveillance for early detection of occupational and work-related diseases and injuries, and notes that workers at risk need regular medical check-ups so the workplace can be modified before permanent damage.
Effective interventions to prevent occupational diseases include ventilation, noise control, and substitution of dangerous chemicals, i.e., controlling hazards at their source.
OSHA's Recommended Practices describe education and training as a core element of an effective safety and health program, alongside hazard identification/assessment and hazard prevention/control.

The Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 established NIOSH as a research agency focused on the study of worker safety and health; NIOSH staff come from fields including medicine, nursing, industrial hygiene, and safety.

Globally, specialized occupational health services reach only about 15% of workers, and more than 85% of workers in small enterprises, the informal sector, agriculture, and among migrants do not have occupational health coverage (WHO fact sheet, November 2017 update).
Chronic respiratory diseases, musculoskeletal disorders, noise-induced hearing loss, and skin problems are among the most common occupational diseases (WHO fact sheet).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'safety hazards' (falls, caught-in machines, struck-by objects) form a separate category from the five WHO-style hazard families.
positions: Some agency topic lists, including OSHA/NIOSH materials, treat safety hazards as their own category alongside chemical, biological, physical, ergonomic, and psychosocial hazards.
The WHO-style grouping used in this lesson folds safety-type dangers (noise, unsafe machines) into the physical family.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the five WHO-style families and keeps safety-type examples (noise, machines) inside the physical family, with one line noting the families overlap; it does not claim the field uses one universal taxonomy.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Vintage of global occupational health coverage statistics.
positions: WHO fact sheet (November 2017 update): specialized occupational health services reach about 15% of workers worldwide; more than 85% of workers in small enterprises, informal sector, agriculture, and migrants lack occupational health coverage.
Newer WHO materials emphasize coverage gaps without repeating identical figures.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson cites the figures with their source and vintage (WHO fact sheet, November 2017 update) rather than presenting them as current data.

correctionsNeeded: No machine-generated draft was reviewed in this session; every claim in the lesson was verified directly against Tier A sources (WHO, CDC/NIOSH via Wayback captures, OSHA, MedlinePlus).
rightsIssues: OSHA and CDC/NIOSH pages are U.S. government works (public domain); WHO pages are WHO-copyrighted and used reference-only, with facts restated in original prose and the working definition attributed and paraphrased. No source prose is reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Occupational health (health topic)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly (who.int served the page). Provides the working definition ('an area of work in public health to promote and maintain highest degree of physical, mental and social well-being of workers in all occupations'), the objectives, and the discipline list (occupational medicine, nursing, ergonomics, psychology, hygiene, safety).

sourceRecords.title: Protecting workers' health (Fact sheet N°389, updated 30 November 2017)
sourceRecords.notes: The current fact-sheet page renders its body client-side and returned no readable content; verified via Internet Archive capture of the earlier canonical WHO copy (https://web.archive.org/web/20190901000000id_/https://www.who.int/mediacentre/factsheets/fs389/en/), which serves the November 2017 update. Supports: workplace health risks (heat, noise, dust, hazardous chemicals, unsafe machines, psychological stress), physical and psychosocial hazards, ergonomic risks, medical surveillance for early detection, source-control interventions (ventilation, noise control, substitution of dangerous chemicals), common occupational diseases, and the coverage figures (services reach about 15% of workers; more than 85% of workers in small enterprises, informal sector, agriculture, and migrants lack coverage).

sourceRecords.title: Hierarchy of Controls
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)
sourceRecords.notes: cdc.gov blocks direct fetch; verified via Wayback capture (https://web.archive.org/web/20230601000000id_/https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/topics/hierarchy/default.html). Supports the five levels in order of general effectiveness (elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, PPE) and the statement that elimination removes the hazard at the source and is preferred because no exposure can occur; also supplies the plant-based-printing-ink substitution example family (lesson uses an original variant).

sourceRecords.title: About NIOSH
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified via Wayback capture (https://web.archive.org/web/20230601000000id_/https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/about/default.html). Supports: the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 established NIOSH as a research agency focused on the study of worker safety and health; NIOSH is part of CDC/HHS; its staff come from fields including epidemiology, medicine, nursing, industrial hygiene, and safety.

sourceRecords.title: About OSHA
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Labor, Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly. Supports OSHA's mission: ensure safe and healthful working conditions free from unlawful retaliation by setting and enforcing standards and providing training, outreach, education, and assistance.

sourceRecords.title: Worker Rights and Protections
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Labor, Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly. Supports: under federal law the employer must keep the workplace free from known safety and health hazards, and workers have the right to workplace safety and health training in a language they understand.

sourceRecords.title: Medical Screening and Surveillance
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Labor, Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly. Supports the existence of OSHA medical screening and surveillance requirements for workplace hazards (e.g., respirator medical evaluation questionnaires, spirometry testing in occupational health programs).

sourceRecords.title: Safety Management: Recommended Practices for Safety and Health Programs
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Labor, Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly. Supports the seven core elements of a safety and health program, including hazard identification and assessment, hazard prevention and control, and education and training, and the goal of preventing workplace injuries, illnesses, and deaths.

sourceRecords.title: Occupational Health
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly. Supports the consumer-level list of occupational health problems (cuts, fractures, sprains; repetitive motion disorders; hearing problems caused by noise; vision problems; illness from breathing, touching, or swallowing unsafe substances; radiation exposure; germs in health care settings) and the prevention practices (set up the work area properly, use the right equipment and gear, reduce stress).
